articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'The Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project' (Digest no.119)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The design to product (DtoP) architecture is built around a central store of product information. The effective operation of DtoP requires that the information it contains is always up to date and accurate. Consequently it is vital that the maintenance of this central store is carefully managed and controlled. The information is accessed by a collection of software tools chosen to suit an application and mediated by a tool manager that overseas the communication between tools and between tools and the information store. The number and complexity of the software tools is variable and can be changed to meet the changing application requirements, as a system and its supported products grow. Only the tool manager and its associated infrastructure tools remain invariant in different systems. The paper deals with this invariant set of tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The Edinburgh Designer System (EDS) is a program intended to provide intelligent support to people engaged in design activities. In supporting the design activity it clearly makes sense to let the program deal with what computers do best while leaving the designer to get on with what (s)he is clearly more capable of. To this end EDS provides support in the generating, recording, and organising of knowledge about a particular design, leaving the designer to make the decisions and intuitive leaps. To organise efforts to implement such support a model of design as an exploration process has been developed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interfacing third party design and manufacturing support tools
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: Addresses one significant element in the successful exploitation of the Alvey design to product large scale demonstrator system (DtoP). That is, a method for the high level integration of DtoP with a company's existing design, manufacturing and in-service support software tools. It describes a prototype general purpose interface which allows a DtoP user to access a 3rd party design analysis tool without a detailed knowledge of the control or capabilities of that tool. A knowledge of both the tool, a mechanical dynamic analysis package, and of the DtoP Designer System, allows the interface to interpret data between the two very different systems intelligently and with a minimum of user intervention. A feature is that when such intervention is necessary, the interface adapts its behaviour to the level of skill and familiarity of that user. It is thus of particular value in reducing familiarisation times.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Problems of designing task-based user interfaces for large-scale CIM systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The research discussed stems from work undertaken within the Alvey research programme in the United Kingdom. The project, design to product (DtoP), was a large scale demonstrator project, whose purpose was to design an innovative, integrated AI-based system covering the design to manufacture process for a complex, mechanical, precision-engineered component. There are a number of major tools in the system, which was build in modular fashion, together with a series of utilities and support tools; the paper concentrates on the work done to develop a user interface to the process planning tool. It describes the methodology adopted to design a series of user interfaces for a range of AI-based tools and their accompanying utilities. It moves on to discuss some of the major issues and problems that arose during the development of these interfaces and some of the conclusions reached.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The 'design to product' Alvey large scale demonstrator
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: As part of the UK government Alvey programme a number of large-scale demonstrators were funded, one of which was the design to product (DtoP) project. Design to Product has been assessing and applying advanced techniques in information technology to computer integrated manufacturing (CIM) with the intention of pathfinding the requirements for the next generation of computer integrated manufacturing implementations. Such systems are envisaged as integrated networks of distributed intelligent facilities supporting all aspects of the company operations and particularly the product lifecycle, from design through manufacturing to in-service operations. Manufacturing companies of the future will require such information systems to improve their manufacturing capabilities and to make optimum use of the limited skills resources available in companies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: Data is passed round the design to product (DtoP) system in the form of data objects. Each object will have a unique system name, belong to a class, contain a number of attributes and may have an attached contents file. A user readable name can be constructed from the attributes. The three main system programs concerned with the handling of data objects are the information management system, the object buffer tool and the working set tool. The browser provides a user interface for selecting objects in the information management system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Solid modelling and its application in DtoP
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: Describes the solid modelling engine (SME), a multi-modeller engine developed at Leeds University. The role of SME in a design to product (DtoP) system is to act as a geometry server. Given well specified input data, the SME performs geometric computations and returns well specified output data. It makes no external calls to other DtoP tools and is therefore completely independent of them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The Loughborough University Manufacturing Planner (LUMP) is a computer aided process planning system based on advanced techniques; its architecture is unique. The incorporation of a rating system where the basic information is rated according to confidence or credibility encourages the exploration of the most promising sets of plans but does not precule exploration of other avenues when appropriate. The author's approach to the problem of process planning is to integrate specialist software within a loose framework and allows the 'experts' to contribute to the solution, he also supports a creative design activity in assisting the process planner to use structured search techniques to explore a potentially very large set of possible plans. LUMP has the ability to link a large number of knowledge sources and to reason about the information they yield, it also enables the use of specialist software. This combination of open multiple context architecture and extensive knowledge engineering allows manufacturing policy to be treated as a design activity rather than a prescriptive path from design to manufacture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The Alvey design to product demonstrator project was carried out at the advanced manufacturing development site of Lucas Diesel Systems at their Gillingham business park factory. After Lucas successful application to become the design to product demonstrator, it was decided that the Gillingham business park site would provide the necessary manufacturing environment required for the project. The article outlines the environment's organisation, manufacturing capability, machine tools and factory control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Alvey 'design to product' demonstrator project: a user's view
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: The paper describes the user's view of design to product (DtoP). The term 'user' is applied to both an organisation using DtoP software for the purposes of demonstration and to the individual engineer interacting with the system at the workstation. It describes both the application-building work undertaken at the demonstration site and reports the limited individual use made of the system. Some observations on the perils of adopting the user role in collaborative projects of this nature are also made.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The generation of assembly data tool
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Alvey 'Design to Product' Demonstrator Project
abstract: Describes the generation of assembly data or GOAD tool that has been developed by the GEC-Marconi Research Centre on the Alvey design to product (DtoP) project. GOAD is integrated into the DtoP system and carries out the assembly process planning activity. The main task of the GOAD tool is to use the product description defined in the designer system to generate the assembly cell program and other information specifying how the product should be assembled on selected assembly cells in the factory. It carries out this task completely automatically by using a knowledge base of assembly planning techniques, assembly methods and equipment capabilities. The GOAD tool uses state of the art assembly planning and knowledge representation techniques that have been developed over the five year period of the project. Unlike similar robot programming systems, GOAD is integrated with a knowledge-based computer aided design system and uses as input a description of the product to automatically plan out and generate the assembly cell programs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
